Furthermore, if both the cause and the fruit were impermanent, then a person at the causal stage could fathom the virtues of the fruit; why, then, would Maitreya have any doubts?
What is clarified here is this: previously, I spoke of the Great for the sake of those who are small, so as to lead the small back to the Great;
now, I speak of the Constant for the sake of those who perceive the inconstant, so as to lead those who perceive the inconstant to realize the Constant.
Furthermore, because the small is inferior while the great is superior, the Great is taught to attract the Small, causing the Small to aspire toward the Great;

because the impermanent is inferior while the permanent is superior, the Permanent is taught to attract the impermanent, causing those who dwell in the impermanent to aspire toward the permanent. Thus, there are two teachings, two conditions, and two distinct stages.
If the Dharma-body were impermanent, the teaching would lack the capacity to induce conditions, and there would be no principle for conditions to rejoice in the teaching.
The fifth section clarifies the dual treatment.
The initial segment clarifies the One Vehicle as distinct from the former Three Vehicles; thus, it takes the three as the "illness" and the one as the "medicine," using the one to exclude the three.

The subsequent chapter clarifies that the present permanence is different from the former impermanence; permanence is the medicine and impermanence is the disease. By using permanence to refute impermanence, there is thus a mutual treatment of the present and the past, as well as the medicine and the disease.

If the latter section still clarifies impermanence, there would be only a treatment for the former and none for the latter; thus, while the former ailment would be dispelled, the subsequent malady would not be removed.
Question:
It is clear that the results also differ from those of the past.
Previously, it was stated that [the kalpas] were eighty or seven hundred *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*; now it is said they are twice that number. Is this not a difference?
Answer: Although it is said that [the lifespan] doubles again, it is ultimately impermanent; the only difference is in its duration.
If it is ultimately impermanent, there will never be a subsequent remedy for it.
If you say that what was short and impermanent in the past is now long and impermanent, yet remains ultimately impermanent;
then it should also follow that what was coarse and threefold in the past is now subtle and threefold, yet remains ultimately threefold.
If three and one are contrasted, then the former three combined would not be three;
likewise, the permanent and the impermanent should also be contrasted, such that what was formerly impermanent is now no longer impermanent.
The sixth point cites two stages in contrast to the two types of birth-and-death.

By previously unifying the three refuges into one, one is exempted from the stage of the two [vehicles]; because those of the human and celestial vehicles enter the One Vehicle, they leave behind the stage of ordinary beings; and because Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas enter the One Vehicle, they leave behind the stage of the two vehicles.

Because one departs from both the stages of ordinary beings and sages, one gives rise to the bodhicitta; by practicing gradually, one enters the ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, ten transferences, and ten grounds, up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment—this constitutes the fulfillment of the meaning of the cause.
If the fruit is still impermanent, one has not yet escaped the two deaths; if one has not yet escaped the two deaths, one has not yet crossed the five hundred yojanas.
If one has already crossed the five hundred yojanas, one has already escaped impermanence.

Furthermore, if the fruit does not yet escape the two deaths, then the fruit is not perfected; if the fruit is not perfected, then the cause of the ten stages is likewise incomplete, and the principle of establishing the cause cannot be established.

What is clarified here is that the first section causes all sentient beings to leave behind the stages of ordinary persons and those of the two vehicles, to resolve upon bodhicitta, and to proceed through the cultivation of the bodhisattva path up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyaksambodhi).
The subsequent chapter clarifies that the fruit eternally eliminates the five stages of dwelling and exhausts the two types of death; thus, the meaning of the fruit is perfected.
Because the cause is fulfilled and the fruit is perfected, this sutra reaches its ultimate conclusion.
The seventh section clarifies the two excellences.
The first part clarifies the excellence of oneness, and the latter part clarifies the excellence of permanence.
Regarding the clarification of the excellence of oneness in the first part: because the Way has no duality, it is called "one."
As the *Avataṃsaka* states: "All those who are fearless give birth to transcendence from life and death through a single path.
There are, however, two senses of this "single path":

first, it is called "one" because there are no differences among the ninety-six heterodox paths; second, it is called "one" because there are no differences among the five vehicles. It is called the "single path" because it is free from these two kinds of distinctions.
Because they are not one, they deviate from the Way and are termed "coarse";
because the Way is non-dual, it is called "sublime.
Thus, the first section correctly demonstrates that all sentient beings share a single, pure Way.

The second section demonstrates that the One Path is eternal: although one knows that the One Path is pure, one has not yet known whether the One Path is eternal or impermanent; therefore, it is next explained that the One Path is eternal.

Because the Way is eternal, it is therefore wondrous; the Tathāgata is one who has realized this single Way. Since the Way is eternal, all Buddhas are also eternal; since the Way is wondrous, those who embody the Way are also wondrous; since the Way is one, those who embody the Way are also one. Thus, the Buddhas of the ten directions share a single Dharma-body.
The reason for this is as follows: if both "non-dharma" and "dharma" are impermanent, then what ultimate difference is there between dharma and non-dharma?

If it were as the ancient teachings claim—that there is only a single "wondrousness" (miao) but no "eternal wondrousness"—then the meaning of "wondrous" would be insufficient, and thus it could not be called the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* (Lotus Sūtra of the True Dharma).
Furthermore, because one path is eternal, that one may be called "sublime. Since it has been clarified from the outset that even this "one" is impermanent, that one is likewise not sublime.
If this is so, then not only is there no sublimity in impermanence, but there is also no sublimity in oneness; since there are no two forms of sublimity, there are only two forms of coarseness.

Now, to clarify that there is only the single true path: it is described according to its meaning; because it reaches the ultimate state of non-duality, it is called "one," and because its essence is neither arising nor ceasing, it is eternal.
Eighth, the clarification of the three inducements.
Throughout the beginning and end of Śākyamuni’s single period of transformation, there are generally three inducements:
that which precedes the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is termed "inducing the heterodox to return to the orthodox."
Before the Buddha appeared in the world, there were two kinds of heterodox teachings:
first, the ninety-six arts of the renunciants who are outside the Way; second, all worldly beings who remain at home.
Although these two types differ from one another, neither constitutes the Buddha-dharma; therefore, they are termed "erroneous.

When the Tathāgata appears in the world, he leads these two erroneous paths back to the correct Dharma of the five vehicles (*pañcayāna*). Among these two types of people, those who have not heard the teachings and follow what is contrary to the Dharma are matured by means of the roots of goodness of humans and devas;

those who possess the spiritual capacities (*gotra*) for the three vehicles are transformed and delivered by means of the Dharma of the three vehicles. Thus, he leads these two erroneous paths back to the correctness of the five vehicles.
Second is "leading the different toward the same.

Although [beings] prior to the *Lotus Sūtra* were spared from the two types of heterodoxy, they still clung to the five distinctions; therefore, the sūtra leads these five distinctions back to the One Vehicle—this is the meaning of the first section.
The third [point] leads the cause back to the fruit.
Although the five vehicles enter the One Vehicle, they still remain at the stage of the cause; therefore, one leads the cause back to the fruit so that the Dharmakāya may be realized.
Just as the śrāvakas attained understanding, the beginning of the ten stages of faith was clarified;
as Maitreya’s doubts were dispelled, the culmination of the ten bhūmis was distinguished.
By citing these two causes—the beginning and the end—one returns to the fruit of the Tathāgata’s ultimate dharmakāya.

These three inductions encompass all that is not included within the unmanifest (avijñapti) and exhaust all meanings without exception; they do not merely apply to Śākyamuni alone, but penetrate through to all Buddhas.
Since these three inductions have been brought to ultimate completion, this is called a "perfect sutra," which is of definitive meaning (nītārtha) and eternally abiding.
Furthermore, there are three stages of leading to the ultimate; therefore, it is explained that those of inferior capacity can attain the Way.
Prior to the *Lotus Sūtra*, there was only the first stage of leading and not yet the second stage; hence, those who attained the Way were few.
If the latter section still clarifies impermanence, there are only two types of inducement and not three.

Furthermore, there is only the inducement of śrāvakas and no inducement of bodhisattvas; because śrāvakas do not believe in the One Vehicle, one now causes them to enter it, and thus only śrāvakas are induced.
Since both Bodhisattvas and Buddhas are equally impermanent, how can one cite Bodhisattvas as an example?
Furthermore, one cannot cite Śrāvakas either.
The reason for this is that all Buddhas and their disciples—the assembly of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—possess bodies that are impermanent; how, then, could they be cited?
Furthermore, if the Buddha were impermanent, it would cause those of the two vehicles to give rise to thoughts of retreat and no longer seek Buddhahood.
Moreover, the three vehicles are likewise impermanent and are termed "half-letters";
as the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "For the sake of the śrāvakas, I speak of half-letters."
This sutra correctly teaches the bodhisattvas; why, then, does it speak of "half-syllables"?
Question:
Since the three [vehicles] lead to the ultimate, for what reason is the *Nirvāṇa* further mentioned?
Answer: There are two kinds of sons:
first, those who do not lose their minds; second, those who lose their minds.
The sons who have not lost their minds hear the three exhortations and all attain realization;

the other sons who have lost their minds do not realize it upon hearing the three exhortations, and thus the Buddha employs the expedient means of proclaiming his extinction to preach *nirvāṇa*, whereby they finally receive the Way.
If that is so, then the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* is taught for those of the most dull faculties.
Question:
If the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* is taught for those of dull faculties, should it not be shallow?
Answer: The teaching is not shallow; however, because realization occurs in dependence upon conditions, it is explained by shifting its emphasis.
It is like a single medicine: one who has not lost their mind takes it first, while one who has lost their mind takes it later.
It is still this same single, correct path; those who are sharp-witted awaken first, while those who are dull-witted awaken later.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Lotus Sūtra* differ in no way.
Question:
If it is said that the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* was taught for those of the most dull faculties, how can the sūtra state, "It was taught for Kāśyapa, the elephant-king among men"?
Answer: One must understand two conditions.

The "condition of not awakening after passing through the teachings" refers to those who, from the time they first saw the Buddha's birth until they heard the *Lotus Sūtra*, still do not attain awakening; these are called people of the most dull faculties, who only attain awakening upon reaching the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

Second, those who have already attained realization previously, but now attain further realization upon reaching the *Nirvāṇa* Sūtra—such as Mahākāśyapa and others of great spiritual faculties—for such people, the *Nirvāṇa* Sūtra is preached.

Furthermore, there are those with faculties who, without hearing the preceding teachings, hear directly of nirvana and immediately possess the full realization of the Tathāgata’s ultimate cause and effect; these are called persons of great sharp faculties.
Question:
Having attained awakening after hearing the preceding teachings one by one, why is this considered dull?
Having attained understanding upon hearing directly of *nirvāṇa*, why is this considered sharp?
Answer:
To hear through various teachings, proceeding from the small to the great and from the shallow to the profound, is called "dull";
to hear directly of the ultimate and attain awakening is called "sharp faculty."
The ninth section clarifies the meaning of the three wheels (*trimaṇḍala*).
The first part opens up the three to reveal the one, referring to the provisional and the real teachings, which is called the Wheel of the Dharma of Teaching (*deśanā-dharmacakra*).
The subsequent chapter distinguishes the opening of the near to reveal the far, which is called the Wheel of Supernatural Powers (*ṛddhi-cakra*).
The Wheel of Dharma refers to all teachings from beginning to end. Although these teachings are numerous, they do not transcend the provisional and the real.
The five vehicles constitute the provisional teaching, while the one vehicle constitutes the real teaching; formerly, the one was divided into five, but now the five are gathered back into the one.
The wheel of supernatural powers refers to all bodies from beginning to end. Although these bodies are numerous, they do not transcend the fundamental body and the manifested body.
Birth at the beginning and extinction at the end, as well as being an ordinary person in the past and a sage in the future, are termed the manifested body.
Without beginning and without end, neither arising nor ceasing—this is called the original body (*mūlakāya*).
In the past, the original manifested through its traces; thus, the original was concealed in order to reveal the traces.
Now, the traces reveal the original; the traces are set aside so that the original may be clarified.
Regarding the wheel of the other’s mind (*paracittacakra*), it penetrates both teachings and both bodies (*kāya*).
Question:
Prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, was there also the doctrine of the three wheels?

Answer: There are likewise three wheels; however, previously, when the Wheel of Dharma was taught, its provisional and ultimate aspects were not yet disclosed, and when the Wheel of Supernatural Powers was taught, the fundamental and manifested dimensions of the body were not yet revealed.
Now, for the first time, both are disclosed together; therefore, it differs from what came before.
The tenth section clarifies two types of exposition:
first, the direct exposition; second, the resolution of doubts to establish the preceding exposition.

Regarding the direct exposition: the initial section clarifies that there are neither ninety-six kinds of heterodox deviations nor five vehicles of orthodox deviations; throughout the three periods of time, all Buddhas possess only a single path.

Regarding the second section, which establishes what was previously stated: although the Way is non-dual, if it were still impermanent, it would be identical to the ninety-six types of paths and likewise identical to the paths of the five vehicles; thus, it could not be called the One Way.
Now it is clarified that the ninety-six paths are, by their very nature, paths of impermanence; now it is clarified that the one path is the path of permanence.

The paths of the five vehicles are called paths of impermanence, whereas the path of the one vehicle alone is the path of permanence; therefore, by citing the path of permanence, the preceding "one path" is established.
Next, the specific clarification of the "exquisite meaning of the cause" is as follows.
The old [commentary] states:

"This sutra only clarifies that the contributing cause (*pratyaya-hetu*) leads to Buddhahood, but has not yet clarified the Buddha-nature as the direct cause (*hetu-hetu*); therefore, even its 'cause' is not yet exquisite."
The commentary states:
This has already been briefly explained above.
As this matter is not insignificant, it shall now be explained in detail.
This sutra distinguishes the coarse from the subtle and differentiates the three forms into one.
In the past there were three vehicles, and thus there were three natures; now there is but the One Vehicle, and thus there is but the One Nature. This is simply the nature of numerical progression.
If they ride upon the One while their natures are three, this is simply because the calculation is incorrect.
Now, let me challenge this:
if they ride upon the One while their natures are three, then since there are already three natures, some sentient beings would attain Buddhahood while others would not.
The reason for this is that while there are the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), there is not even one single nature; therefore, things may either be established or not established.
If this is so, how can the sutra state: "Even a single hair's worth of goodness leads to Buddhahood"?

Furthermore, if there were those who could attain Buddhahood despite lacking the nature of the One Vehicle (ekayāna-gotra) in the present, then there should have been those who attained the three vehicles despite lacking the nature of the three vehicles (triyāna-gotra) in the past.
Moreover, since there were the three natures in the past, there was the principle of attaining the three [vehicles];
but now that the one nature is absent, there is no principle for attaining the one.

Furthermore, if there is no single vehicle-nature (ekayāna-gotra) yet one becomes [a single vehicle], then since the three natures (tri-svabhāva) are equally non-existent, why does one not become three?

Moreover, regarding the fact that even in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, although the single vehicle is elucidated, the three natures still persist: this would mean that while the vehicle is one, the natures remain three.
If one were to ride upon the One while its nature is Three, then previously one would have ridden upon the Three while its nature was One.
It is impossible to ride upon the Three while its nature is One; how then could one ride upon the One while its nature is Three?
Furthermore, to ride upon the One while its nature is Three is a contradiction in fact, which no wise person would believe.
For example, if it has already become only a single flavor, how can you further say that milk has five natures?
If milk has five natures, how can it be said to consist of only one flavor?
If it consists of only one flavor, why do you further claim that its natures are five?
One who possesses even a slight discernment of the subtleties of salt and plum, and who is not quite the same as wood or stone, would not speak these words.
If the words themselves cannot be established, how can their meaning possibly stand?

If you claim that the present teaching lacks the three vehicles of nature while the former teaching possessed the three natures, then it should also follow that the present teaching possesses the one vehicle of nature while the former teaching lacked the one nature; this too is merely a matter of numerical parity.

If you say that now you clarify there are no three natures, and further clarify there is not even one nature, then since the three natures do not exist, the Three Vehicles cannot be established; and if there is not even one nature, how could anything be established?

If one were to say that the Buddha did not teach the existence of a single-vehicle nature (*ekayāna-gotra*), nor did he clarify the absence of such a nature, but merely spoke of attaining Buddhahood through the single vehicle by way of a concealed teaching (*saṃvṛti-nirdeśa*), then since there would be no causal conditions for attaining Buddhahood, by what means could one possibly become a Buddha?

Now, in discussing the attainment of Buddhahood, there must necessarily be its underlying principle: sentient beings possess the inherent capacity for Buddhahood, and thus they can indeed become Buddhas.
If one does not understand whether this capacity exists or not, by what means could Buddhahood be achieved?
For example, whether yellow stone contains gold or not, it would be unheard of to suddenly command people to smelt it in a furnace.
Question:
This sutra states below, "The Honored One among two-legged beings, humans and devas, knows that dharmas are eternally without intrinsic nature."
"Since it has been stated that there is no nature, how can one speak of the nature of the One Vehicle?
Answer: This merely clarifies the refutation of the attachment to [the notion of] a nature.
Furthermore, this refutes the views of the non-Buddhists and those of the Hīnayāna who assert that the nature exists within the cause.
If it is as the Buddha-nature described in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, how could one say that it does not exist?
Furthermore, an objection is raised:
"If there is no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then there should likewise be no distinct Buddha-lineage that differs from the lineages of the three vehicles;
yet now there exists a distinct lineage that differs from the lineages of the five vehicles. For what reason, then, is there no distinct nature that differs from the three natures?"
If it is said that the myriad practices lack an inherent nature as their seeds, then since these myriad practices lack an inherent nature, why must they lead to Buddhahood?
Furthermore, if there is no Buddha in a single practice, there is likewise no Buddha in the myriad practices;
yet, if the myriad practices together constitute Buddhahood, why does a single practice not do so as well? Why is it not achieved?
Nāgārjuna said: "If a jar can emerge from within clay, why do carriages, horses, food, and drink not likewise emerge from the tip of a finger?

Furthermore, if you say that the Buddha-nature was not taught because one's past grasping at a self had not yet been eliminated, then why did you not fear that one would fail to attain Buddhahood in the present, and instead teach that the nature exists?
One should not be timid when looking back at what has passed, nor bold when anticipating what lies ahead.
By inferring from these various matters, one must know that one should clarify the Buddha-nature and should preach upon the Buddha-nature.
The reason for this is that the Buddha-nature is the foundation of the Buddha-vehicle; because the Buddha-nature exists, it is manifested through conditions.
To explain only the causal conditions while failing to speak of the fundamental nature is to abandon the root and grasp at the branches—a mark of lack of wisdom.
Furthermore, since Vasubandhu already clarified the Buddha-nature in his commentary on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, how much more so would he have done so in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*?

Moreover, five years after his enlightenment, [the Buddha] preached the *Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra* to clarify the existence of the Buddha-nature; how much more so, then, would it not have been clarified in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*?
If you say that this should not be cited because it is not a sequential teaching, could one then claim that the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* was also taught without a fixed sequence?

If you say that Vasubandhu and others are not to be trusted, then on what basis do you accept the "Five Periods" (pañcakāla), which were composed by Huiguan, and the "Four Tenets" (catuḥsiddhānta), which were the writings of Daoping?
To oppose the sages and follow the ordinary is truly something I cannot understand.

If you claim that because there is no textual passage on Buddha-nature it should not be employed, then since the *Nirvāṇa* and *Avataṃsaka* Sūtras contain no mention of the ālayavijñāna, these two sūtras would likewise fail to clarify the eight consciousnesses; therefore, one cannot expect a single scripture to encompass the entirety of all teachings.
In that case, there would be only one category; how could the eight directions be established?
Because all possess Buddha-nature, they cultivate practice and attain Buddhahood; therefore, this is wondrous.
If there were no Buddha-nature, one would not attain Buddhahood; therefore, it would not be wondrous.
Next, the lifespan is discussed specifically.
The older tradition states:
from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* through to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, [the Buddha] was entirely impermanent.
By what reasoning do you prove that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is eternal?
The critique states:
We now provide three proofs.
First, the scriptural evidence from a sutra prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*:
Vasubandhu, in his *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, states: "Because the three marks have distinct natures, the Tathāgata is that which is apart from those three marks."
This clarifies that the three characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing are distinct from the Dharma-body; apart from those three characteristics is the Tathāgata’s single Dharma-body.
Thus, one knows that the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā* has already clarified the meaning of permanence; how much more so could the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, which follows it, be impermanent?
If the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* were to appear later and be impermanent, then the *Prajñāpāramitā* would be superior and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* inferior.
The "Sadāprarudita Chapter" of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "The form-bodies (*rūpakāya*) of all Buddhas come and go; the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) neither comes nor goes."
Thus, it is clear that the Dharma-body is eternal; how much more so in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*?

The *Prajñāpāramitā Hṛdaya Sūtra* (or *Kṣudraprajñāpāramitā*) clearly distinguishes that the Dharma-body cannot be transmigrated or extinguished, which is in agreement with the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
The third, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, states: "The Buddha-body is without outflows (*anāsrava*), for all [defilements] have been exhausted.
The Buddha-body is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), not following after any numerical categories.
These two sentences fully explain the eternal body of the Tathāgata.
Question:
How do these two fully elucidate the dharmakāya? Answer:
That the Buddha’s body is without outflows means that the fetters of the cause have been severed.
That the Buddha’s body is unconditioned and does not fall into any numerical categories means that the bonds of the fruit have been severed.
Since both the cause and the fruit have been severed, is it not indeed eternal?
Furthermore, because the Buddha’s body is without outflows (*anāsrava*), it differs from the bodies of ordinary beings;
because the Buddha’s body is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it differs from the impermanent bodies of the two vehicles.
Therefore, the Buddha’s body is eternal and constant, without change or alteration.
Furthermore, the Buddha’s body is without outflows (*anāsrava*), as all five stages of dwelling have been overturned;
the Buddha’s body is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), as it is free from both forms of death.
This distinguishes it from the body of a bodhisattva.

From the Bodhisattva’s initial aspiration until the attainment of the Diamond-like Samādhi, as long as even a single moment of ignorance has not been severed, they are still said to possess outflows and impermanence;
as long as the retribution of suffering remains, they are not termed unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The Buddha has already transcended these, and is therefore eternal.
Furthermore, the Buddha’s body is without outflows and thus cannot be said to exist;
the Buddha’s body is unconditioned and thus cannot be said not to exist.
Neither existent nor non-existent, this is the Middle Way, the Dharma-body;
therefore, it is called "eternal. If it were either of the two extremes, it would be called "impermanent.

Furthermore, the Buddha-body being without outflows is liberation; the Buddha-body being unconditioned refers to the Dharma-body and Prajñā. Although these are pointed out as three, they do not transcend the attainment of liberation and the possession of the three virtues; therefore, it is called eternal.

Furthermore, the Buddha-body is called "empty" because it is without outflows (*anāsrava*), and it is called "not empty" because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Therefore, the Great Nirvāṇa possesses the meanings of both emptiness and non-emptiness; this is precisely what is meant by "permanence."
If even the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* clarifies that the Dharma-body is eternal, how much more so the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*?
Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrti* states: "O virtuous ones!
This body is impermanent; you should take delight in the Buddha-body."

Since it has been stated that this body is impermanent and one should take delight in the Buddha-body, yet the Buddha-body is likewise impermanent and identical to one's own body, what is there to delight in?
Question:
The introduction to the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* clarifies the permanence of the Dharma-body, yet this is not the main thesis of the sutra itself.
Answer: This is the question of a fool.

What you have received is that which was taught in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*; all of it constitutes the core tenets (*siddhānta*) of the *Vimalakīrti* scripture. How can you say that it is not the orthodox teaching?
Therefore, Master Sengzhao said:
"From the beginning in the Pure Land to the end with the offerings, although the texts differ, the inconceivable is one.
Furthermore, since this is not the core tenet of the sūtra, it would contradict that core tenet; how then can it be explained?
Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* consists of two locations and four assemblies.
As for the two locations: first, the location of the garden retreat (*ārāma*); second, the location of the chamber (*vargavastu*). As for the four assemblies:

the first assembly at the garden retreat in the "Buddhakṣetra-parivarta"; the first assembly at the chamber in the "Upāya-parivarta"; the subsequent assembly at the chamber beginning from the "Glan-pa dri-ba" (Vimalakīrti’s Inquiry on Illness) chapter; and the subsequent assembly at the garden retreat beginning from the "Bodhisattvacaryā-parivarta" chapter.
If that is so, since the "Expedient Means" chapter was preached within the inner chamber, why do you say it is not the primary teaching of the sutra?
Furthermore, if the introduction to the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* contradicts its main exposition, then all other sutras would necessarily be the same.
Furthermore, Zixia’s preface to the *Shijing* and Yuan-kai’s prefaces to the commentaries all deviate from the orthodox scriptures.
Next, he cites the text of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to substantiate his threefold explanation by means of the three types of realization.
The "Expedient Means" chapter elucidates a single mode of teaching:
first, it extensively distinguishes between the provisional and the real aspects of the teachings; second, it briefly clarifies the fundamental and manifested aspects of the Buddha-body.
As it says, "There is only the One Vehicle Dharma," which refers to the Real Teaching; "expediently teaching the Three Vehicles," which refers to the Provisional Teaching.

"I first sat at the site of enlightenment" refers to the manifested body (*trikāya*); "from kalpas long ago" praises and reveals the Dharma of *nirvāṇa*, referring to the original body (*dharmakāya*).
Śāriputra further summarizes these two matters:

the first passage understands the provisional and ultimate aspects of the teaching; the subsequent statement, "Just as the World-Honored One now—from birth, renunciation, attaining the Way, and turning the wheel of Dharma—also speaks by means of skillful means," summarizes the original and manifested aspects of the Buddha's person.
Since it is said that arising from birth and leaving the household life constitutes the provisional trace-body, then non-arising and non-ceasing must constitute the real body.

Since arising and ceasing are taken as the trace-body, and the trace-body is impermanent, while non-arising and non-ceasing constitute the fundamental body, and the fundamental body is eternal—this is one explanation and its corresponding understanding.
Next, the "Parable Chapter" clarifies that the three carts represent the provisional teaching, while the single cart represents the ultimate teaching.
The Tathāgata has already departed from all afflictions of cause and effect and is endowed with all virtues; this is called the Dharma-body.
That he was born into the decayed and dilapidated fire-houses of the triple world refers to the *traces-body* (*traces of the Buddha*).
Furthermore, it says, "At that time, the elder stood outside the gate," which refers to the *dharma-body*.
"Startled, he enters the burning house" refers to the manifested body (*trikāya*).
Since the manifested body attains enlightenment through the eight phases within the triple world, it possesses birth and extinction.
The fundamental body (*mūlakāya*) exists outside the triple world; therefore, it is without birth or extinction.
The "Chapter on Faith and Understanding" summarizes two matters:
first, the "messenger" refers to the teaching of reality (the *śuddha-dharma*); second, the "messenger" refers to the provisional teaching (*upāya-dharma*).
"The elder’s adornment" refers to his original body; "removing his precious, noble robes and donning tattered, soiled garments" refers to his manifested trace-body.
Question:
This clarification of the fundamental and the manifested is indeed as you have stated.
How, then, can this be used to prove what is permanent and what is impermanent?
Answer: We now ask the Elder: surrounded by your retinue, are you the Dharma-body or the Response-body?
If you are the Dharma-body, how can there be a retinue surrounding you, or coming and going, taking and giving?
Furthermore, why do you say he stayed in a single city?
As for this emanation body (nirmāṇakāya) of Śākyamuni, who cast off his precious and noble robes to don tattered and soiled garments—what kind of body does this further metaphorize?
What is clarified here is that the elder’s adornment is the body of Śākyamuni,
while his coming and going, taking and giving, refers to the teaching of Śākyamuni.
If this is so, since the form and teaching of Śākyamuni are contained within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, does not the teaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* indeed proclaim permanence?
Furthermore, why do you say these are "half-letters"?
If the *Lotus Sūtra* were a teaching of impermanence consisting of half-letters, then the doctrinal meaning of Śākyamuni Buddha’s teachings would likewise have to be so.
Question:
Where in this [text] is there a passage concerning the permanence of the dharmakāya? Answer:
The cessation within one city is the Nirmāṇakāya (the Response Body), while that which precedes this cessation is the Dharmakāya (the Dharma Body).
Therefore, since the Dharmakāya manifests the traces of Śākyamuni, the Dharmakāya is eternal.
Question:
In which part of Śākyamuni’s teaching is there a textual passage concerning the three bodies? Answer:
The *Sūtra on Resolving Doubts Concerning the Semblance Dharma* states: "In some instances, one sees my body as Vairocana, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of Śākyamunis;
in others, one sees my body filling all of space—this is the Dharmakāya; and in others, one sees it as sixteen feet tall—this is the Nirmāṇakāya."
Question:
One should only understand and accept two bodies; why does this sutra instead lead one to understand and accept three bodies? Answer:
This sutra comprehensively explains the beginning and end of the single transformation; therefore, it fully encompasses the three bodies (trikāya).
There are separate topical outlines for each of the three bodies.
The third cycle also possesses two types of teaching, wherein the provisional and the real are easily understood.
As it is said, "In other lands I act as a Buddha under different names," this clarifies the fundamental and manifested aspects of the body (shin-honjaku).
Although not explicitly stated in the section on "Accepting and Understanding" (ryōge), it may be understood by analogy with what precedes.
Question:
If that is so, since the three cycles fully clarify the physical form, the teachings, and the lifespan, why is there such prolixity in the explanation? Answer:
In the first cycle of teaching, the bodies are extensive while the teachings are concise; in the latter cycle, the bodies are concise while the teachings are extensive.
Furthermore, in the first cycle, the two bodies are presented to establish the two teachings, whereas in the latter cycle, the two teachings are presented to establish the two bodies.
Next, regarding the realization of the two types of *nirvāṇa*, this is a brief explanation of the meaning of *nirvāṇa*.
There are generally three differences between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna *nirvāṇas*:

first, the difference between being intrinsically quiescent and not being intrinsically quiescent; second, the difference in severing the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms, both internal and external; and third, the difference between possessing all virtues and not possessing all virtues.

Regarding the statement that "intrinsic quiescence is not different from non-intrinsic quiescence," the "Expedient Means" chapter says: "I have established these expedient means to speak of the paths for exhausting all suffering and to point them toward nirvana; yet even this is not ultimate extinction."
This clarifies the nirvāṇa of past skillful means:
"All dharmas, from the very beginning, are eternally of the nature of quiescent extinction.
Once the Son of the Buddha has practiced the Way, he shall become a Buddha in a future age."
This clarifies that the present teaching concerns the true *nirvāṇa*.
Question:
What is the difference between these two types of *nirvāṇa*?
Answer: This has already been clarified within the text.
However, some people claim that this is a passage concerning the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) rather than the *Nirvāṇa*.

Now, it is clarified that this is not so; the scriptural text directly contrasts the small nirvāṇa with the great nirvāṇa. The small nirvāṇa serves as a skillful means, while the great nirvāṇa is the ultimate reality. Therefore, the preceding phrase clarifies what is not the ultimate reality, and the subsequent phrase clarifies true cessation.
Question:
How do these two types of nirvana reveal the provisional and the real? Answer:
As the Sūtra itself states, because those of the Hīnayāna extinguish afflictions, it is called "small nirvāṇa.
In the Mahāyāna, it is said that "all dharmas are from the very beginning characterized by eternal quiescence," and for this reason it is called "great nirvāṇa."
Question:
Why is the cessation of afflictions called "small," while primordial quiescence is called "great"?
Answer:

The followers of the Hīnayāna do not know that afflictions and the body are fundamentally unborn from the beginning and are likewise without cessation now; thus, they perceive the arising of afflictions and seek to extinguish them. This is a contemplation of arising and ceasing, and for this reason it is called "small."

Mahāyāna practitioners know that afflictions are fundamentally unarisen from the beginning and are likewise without cessation; because they observe them through the lens of non-arising and non-ceasing, it is called Great Nirvāṇa.
Question:
By what means is it further proven that followers of the Hīnayāna do not know that [afflictions] are fundamentally unarisen and do not cease?
Answer: The preceding text serves as clear evidence, and the meaning can be understood from it.

Furthermore, the *Śāstra* states: "The gate of emptiness in the Mahāyāna refers to the fact that all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*) and empty of intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnya*)."
"Those of the Lesser Vehicle who follow the gate of emptiness clarify emptiness by means of the refutation of phenomena.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "Because people of the Lesser Vehicle do not know that the nature of all phenomena is empty, they do not attain the suchness of the selflessness of phenomena."
Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* states: "For those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*), the Buddha teaches that the severance of the three poisons is called nirvāṇa.
If one is free from overweening pride, the Buddha teaches that the three poisons themselves are nirvāṇa."
Regarding the statement that "the three poisons are themselves nirvāṇa": since the three poisons are fundamentally unarisen and do not now cease, are they not indeed nirvāṇa?

Furthermore, the *Dharmapada-śāstra* (*Fahua lun*), in explaining the meaning of the existence or non-existence of the Two Vehicles versus the One Vehicle, clarifies that there is no nirvāṇa for the Two Vehicles, but only the Great Nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata.
Thus we know that this sutra distinguishes *nirvāṇa* from that of the Hīnayāna. If this is so, is the body then the same as it was before?

Second, to clarify the difference between the *nirvāṇa* of the Hīnayāna and that of the Mahāyāna: in the "Parable Chapter," it is said that those of the Hīnayāna merely distance themselves from delusions and thus call it liberation; in reality, they have not attained complete liberation. That which is called "delusion" refers to the seeds and fruits within the triple world; because the two vehicles have escaped these, they are said to have attained liberation.
Regarding "complete liberation" (*sarvavimukti*): it is called complete liberation because all sons and fruits, both internal and external to the three realms, are entirely detached from them.
Therefore, there is a difference in meaning between the Great and Small [Vehicles] regarding the concepts of "short" and "long" *nirvāṇa*.
Question:

In the Hīnayāna, the cessation of the bonds of the "sons" (sentient beings) of the three realms is called *sopadhiśeṣa* (with remainder), and the cessation of the bonds of the "fruits" (defilements) of the three realms is called *nirupadhiśeṣa* (without remainder).
How is it further explained in the Mahāyāna?
Answer:

The exhaustion of all bonds of the "seeds" (hetu-bandhana) within and without the three realms is called "with remainder" (sopadhiśeṣa); the exhaustion of all bonds of the "fruits" (phala-bandhana) within and without the three realms is called "without remainder" (nirupadhiśeṣa).
Question:
In the Hīnayāna, one first attains the state with remainder and subsequently enters the state without remainder; how is it in the Mahāyāna? Answer:
This refers to "at one time.
Since the ignorance that obstructs Buddhahood has been severed, the retribution of impermanence and suffering is immediately purified; therefore, the two types of nirvana are simultaneous.
This is excerpted from the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
Third, to clarify the difference between the Great and Small Nirvāṇas: the Nirvāṇa of the Hīnayāna does not possess all virtues, whereas the Nirvāṇa of the Mahāyāna is fully endowed with all virtues.
As stated in the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding": "For a long night we have practiced the dharma of emptiness and attained liberation from the afflictions and sufferings of the triple world."
In the Nirvāṇa of the Hīnayāna, it is called "emptiness" because it lacks both body and wisdom; it is called "emptiness" because there is only the dharma and no person.
Great Nirvāṇa, however, is fully endowed with body, wisdom, person, and dharma.
Therefore, the "Chapter on Resolute Belief" states: "The King of all dharmas, which are untainted and unconditioned.

This passage encompasses all meanings: because they are untainted (*anāsrava*), they refer to the virtue of liberation; because they are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), they possess the virtues of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

The untainted and unconditioned is the Dharma, and the King of all Dharmas is the person; therefore, one knows that the Tathāgata’s body—being untainted and unconditioned—is Nirvāṇa, wherein both person and Dharma are fully perfected.
The "Chapter on Resolute Belief" has not yet fully explained this meaning.

Furthermore, the "Chapter on Parables" clarifies that the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa differs from the nirvāṇa of the two vehicles, as it says: "All are brought to extinction by means of the Tathāgata’s extinction; no one is allowed to attain extinction alone."
This clarifies the difference between the two types of cessation—great and small—which is precisely the difference between the fruit and the fruit-of-fruit.
It further states: "All these sentient beings who have escaped the triple world are provided with the requisites for the enjoyment of the meditative concentrations and liberations of all Buddhas."
This clarifies that the virtues of the Buddha’s assembly differ from those of the two vehicles; thus, the meaning of the "fruit" (*phala*) differs.
Question:

Why does the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* first clarify the fruit and subsequently distinguish the fruit-of-the-fruit (*phalaphala*), whereas the text of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* first clarifies the fruit-of-the-fruit and subsequently distinguishes the fruit?
Answer: The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* clarifies that the Buddha’s two fruits are identical to those in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

However, the difference between the two scriptures is as follows: the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* addresses those of the Hīnayāna who take the preservation of cessation as the ultimate truth; it seeks to replace their minor cessation with the Great Cessation, just as one replaces a small cart with a great vehicle. Therefore, it first elucidates the Great Cessation.
The followers of the Hīnayāna do not regard other virtues as supreme; hereafter, other virtues will be clarified.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states, "I wish to praise nirvāṇa"; therefore, nirvāṇa is inscribed as the fruit among fruits, occupying the final position.
Furthermore, these two realities have no sequence of before or after; they are merely distinguished according to their respective meanings.
Question:
By citing the differences between the two types of nirvāṇa, what do you intend to clarify?
Answer: This is intended to illustrate the difference between the two bodies.
Since the two types of nirvāṇa—Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna—are distinct, the two dharma-bodies of Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are likewise distinct.

The fivefold dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya*) of the Hīnayāna is a body subject to arising and ceasing and is impermanent; the Dharma-body of the Mahāyāna refers to a body that is eternally free from arising and ceasing.
If this sutra were to clarify that the Dharma-body is still impermanent, then it would likewise have to clarify that Nirvāṇa is no different from that of the Hīnayāna.
Question:
This sutra clarifies that nirvana is no different from what was taught in the past.
How is this known to be so?
This sutra clarifies that since the Buddha is impermanent, he ultimately enters *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, which is the same as in the Hīnayāna.
Furthermore, the first chapter states: "The Buddha passes into parinirvāṇa this night, like a fire extinguished when its fuel is exhausted. Thus, we know it is no different from the Hīnayāna.
The critique states:
This is a matter of great importance and should be carefully deliberated and finalized.

Previously, you cited the "Expedient Means" and "Parable" chapters, where the Buddha himself stated that the two types of nirvana—the Great and the Small—are distinct. Why, then, do you contradict the Buddha’s own words by claiming they are not different?
Such a person is one who lacks faith.
Furthermore, an objection is raised:
"If the Great and Small Vehicles share the same *nirvāṇa*, then the cause would differ while the fruit remains the same; this is not possible."
Furthermore, both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna fundamentally aim for the fruit; since they are identical in their goal, why should their causes differ?
What is clarified here is that because the two causes differ, the two fruits likewise differ;
yet there is no further divergent cause, as they ultimately converge upon a single cause, and no further divergent fruit, as they ultimately converge upon a single fruit.
Question:

This sutra states, "Tonight the Buddha enters parinirvāṇa, like a fire extinguished when its fuel is exhausted. Is this not the nirvana of the Hīnayāna, characterized by the cessation of the ashes? How can it be said to be the Mahāyāna nirvana?

Answer: Regarding the statement that "the fire is extinguished when the fuel is exhausted," the stimulus is taken as the fuel and the response is taken as the fire; therefore, when the stimulus is exhausted, the response simply ceases.
Question:
How is this known to be so? Answer:

The "Chapter on Lifespan" states, "By the power of skillful means, it is said that there is both extinction and non-extinction. How could this be the same as the two vehicles' [view] of extinguishing the body and extinguishing wisdom, like the extinction of fire when the fuel is exhausted?
Furthermore, when conditions are exhausted, that which corresponds to them must necessarily cease; this is simply the nature of numerical calculation.
As the *Mahā-sūtra* states: "This is the natural law of all Buddhas, and it is likewise for all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*)."
Question:
Some say, "All dharmas have from the beginning been of the nature of eternal quiescence. This clarifies that the quiescence of the One Vehicle is the characteristic of the Three Vehicles.
Why do you now equate this with *nirvāṇa*?
Answer: This is merely a matter of human sentiment and convention; it is not the meaning of the Buddha’s teaching.

The preceding verse in the Buddhist sutra clarifies that this is not true extinction, while the subsequent verse distinguishes true extinction. How, then, can this be correlated with the meaning of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna)?

If this passage were intended to clarify that the One Vehicle (ekayāna) lacks the three marks [of arising, abiding, and ceasing], then the preceding text should have stated that the Three Vehicles do not constitute true cessation; it should not have stated that Nirvana is not true cessation.
Question:
Now you are precisely elucidating the three vehicles and the one vehicle; why then do you explain nirvāṇa? Answer:
It is precisely because *nirvāṇa* differs that the three vehicles and the one vehicle are distinguished.

This is truly because the *nirvāṇa* of the one vehicle is true cessation, whereas the *nirvāṇa* of the three vehicles is not true cessation; therefore, the one vehicle is the true vehicle, while the three vehicles are not the true vehicle.
If one does not distinguish the three [vehicles] from the One by means of something other than *nirvāṇa*, what else could be used for such a distinction?
Many who lecture on the sūtras are confused at this point; I hope they will examine the text with careful observation.
Furthermore, some say:

"As for the statement that 'all dharmas have from the very beginning been characterized by constant quiescence,' the first section opened up the three vehicles to reveal the One, yet it did not yet speak of the treasure-store of nirvāṇa."

Therefore, for the time being, following the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, we take the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as nirvāṇa; thus it is said that [all phenomena] are quiescent and extinguished from the very beginning.
Evaluation: This, too, is not so.

If the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and the *Daśabhūmika-śāstra* explicitly clarify that intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) constitutes the Mahāyāna nirvāṇa, this is precisely the aspect of original quiescence in the present text.
Since that treatise has already explained ultimate *nirvāṇa*, we know that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* distinguishes the perfectly consummate and true cessation (*bhūtanirodha*).
Question:
For what reason are all people dark while you alone are enlightened?

Answer: The first interpretation restricts [the teaching] to five periods, while the latter explanation judges it by means of two sections; because they did not carefully examine the text, they missed its subtle purport.
Next, the old explanations from Guan and He are cited to corroborate the meaning of permanence and impermanence.
In the past, when Dharmarakṣa translated the old version of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, its central tenets had not yet been definitively established.
Since the new version was translated by Kumārajīva, Dharma Master Sengrui of Chang’an personally assisted him during the translation process.
The "Preface" to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "Because his lifespan is immeasurable, even eternal kalpas are insufficient to clarify its duration;
because his manifested bodies are innumerable, ten thousand forms are insufficient to differentiate his essence."

Thus, the measure of his lifespan is determined to be beyond calculation; his manifested bodies clarify that he is not substantial; Samantabhadra reveals that he has no coming; and Prabhūtaratna testifies that he does not perish.
The critique states:
"That Master Rui personally received [the teachings from] Kumārajīva and composed this preface is itself clear evidence that [the Lotus Sūtra] is eternal.
Since it is the fundamental source of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, one cannot help but rely upon it."

Next, Dao Lang of Hexi translated the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* in response; he was also the author of the *Fahua Tonglüe*, which clearly explains that there are five general intentions for expounding the *Lotus Sūtra*.

The fourth interpretation states: "It is to clarify that the true body and the manifested body of the Dharma-body are not different, and that their existence and disappearance share a single principle, as explained in the 'Muchilinda' chapter.
Since sentient beings do not understand this, this sutra is preached in order to reveal this meaning."
It is further stated: "The manifestation of the Stūpa of Many Treasures clarifies that the Dharma-body eternally abides;
the 'Chapter on the Lifespan' clarifies that its measure is equal to the great void.
The critique says:

Daolang authored the *Nirvāṇa-śū*, which was widely circulated in his time; his interpretation of the *Lotus Sūtra* was not erroneous in its principles, and his elucidation of the doctrine of permanence accorded with that of Master Sengrui.
Daochang Huiquan said:
"The three assemblies going together and returning as one is the beginning of the vehicle;
the dissolution of form and clarification of the spirit is the end of the vehicle."
"Extinguishing the shadow means stilling the traces; clarifying the spirit then reveals the fundamental source. Thus, while the traces are impermanent, the source is eternal.
The critique states:
"This is essentially the same as Master Rui’s interpretation."

Next, in the commentary on the *Lotus Sūtra*, it says: "That which is not subject to the reckoning of existence or extinction is called 'longevity' (śu); it transcends the limits of longevity or premature death.

This clarifies that the Dharma-body is not encompassed by physical form or years; it causes the Mahāsattva to cultivate and realize the ultimate illumination, such that one does not become a Buddha merely at Gayā, nor does one take a hundred years as the measure of a full life."
The critique states:
This commentary further clarifies the doctrine of permanence, yet its purport is exceedingly pure and profound. Why is this so?

Since it is said to be neither existent nor non-existent, this is precisely non-arising and non-ceasing, neither cultivated nor destroyed, neither permanent nor impermanent; it is no different from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra’s* elucidation of the Dharma-body as transcending the hundred negations.
Next, Zhu Daosheng said:
"As for the Buddha of the form-body (*rūpakāya*), he exists through manifestation and response; he possesses no substantial form.
Since his form is not real, how could there be a lifespan?"

Thus, the myriad forms reach the same destination, and antiquity and the present are one; the past is the present, and the present is the past. There is no time when they do not exist, and no place where they are not present.
If there were times when he was not present or places where he was not located, this would apply only to ordinary sentient beings; it is not so for the Buddha.
Therefore, it is definitively resolved that his lifespan is exceedingly long, and Gayā is indeed such a place.
Gaya is this, yet it is no longer Gaya; since Gaya is not that "long," how could it alone be so? When both long and short perish, both long and short persist.
The critique states:
"Dàolǎng and Sēngruì merely elucidated the meaning of permanence;
Master Shēng’s commentary on the sutra elucidates the meaning of being neither permanent nor impermanent."
Both "permanence" and "impermanence" are merely refutations of specific ailments; they belong to the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of therapeutic remedies).
The *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the standpoint of ultimate truth) is the Dharmakāya. How could the Dharmakāya be grasped through the five propositions such as permanence, impermanence, and so forth?
Question:
The "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter states: "Ultimate nirvana is the mark of eternal quiescence; it ultimately returns to emptiness.
Does this not mean that one finally enters the nirvana without remainder, relinquishing both the impermanent body and wisdom?
The critique states:
Guangzhai’s statement fails to understand the meaning of the text.

If he claims that this sutra clarifies that the emptiness of nirvāṇa is precisely the wisdom that extinguishes the body, then how could it be consistent with the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*’s assertion that "great nirvāṇa is empty"? Could that indeed be so?
Furthermore, if both body and wisdom were ultimately impermanent, how would they differ from those of the Two Vehicles?
Now, it is clarified that the "Chapter on the Herbs" explicitly presents two ultimate states, citing two fruits:

first, the initial passage states, "Ultimately reaching all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*). This cites the ultimate fruit of wisdom, demonstrating that the wisdom of those in the Two Vehicles is not ultimate.
The second point states: "Ultimate nirvana is a state of eternal quiescence, ultimately returning to emptiness.
This cites the ultimate cessation [of the two vehicles] to reveal that the cessation achieved by those of the two vehicles is not ultimate.
Having already clarified these two meanings, the preceding and following sections thus open with two distinct texts.
Because the latter clarifies the ultimate cessation, *nirvāṇa* is empty and devoid of all marks.
Question:
How is it known that both the fruit and the fruit-of-the-fruit are being presented? Answer:

In the "Parable Chapter," the great chariot is combined with two fruits; both are described as the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa. Here, "parinirvāṇa" refers to the fruit of fruits, while the wisdom and concentration of all Buddhas refer to the fruit itself.
Although the virtues of the Buddha are many, none transcend these two.
Furthermore, Master Daorong was a proponent of the *Lotus Sūtra*;
he stated that "the Great Nirvāṇa is empty and devoid of all marks" and also that "emptiness is free from afflictions," which accords with our present intention.
Master Yin said:
"In the end, it returns to the eternally abiding, primary emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). Master Zhong said:
"It ultimately culminates in the wisdom of the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
Furthermore, others say: "The fruit of Buddhahood is empty because it is free from all attachments."
The commentary on the sutra states: "When both emptiness and existence are equally exhausted, this is what is called 'emptiness'.
The critique says:

Previous Dharma Masters all claimed that the eternally abiding is empty and signless; however, the intent of this commentary may transcend those prior judgments, asserting that it is called "emptiness" because both emptiness and existence are utterly transcended.
Question:
Since you speak of a "measure of lifespan," could it not be permanent? Answer:
If that were so, then being called "Immeasurable Life" (Amitāyus) would imply it is permanent.
Since the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states that Immeasurable Life is not permanent, how could the lifespan now explained here possibly be impermanent?
Now, it is clarified that there are four propositions:
First, it is actually finite, yet because its excellence is praised as being exceedingly long, it is called "immeasurable," as in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.

Second, it is actually immeasurable; because one wishes to clarify that its measure is equal to the great void, it is called "life-span" (*āyus-pramāṇa*), which refers to this very sūtra, and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama Sūtra* is likewise.
Third, it is truly immeasurable yet described as immeasurable, as the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "Only a Buddha perceives a Buddha, and his lifespan is immeasurable.
Fourth, it is measurable yet described as measurable, as when it is said that Śākyamuni’s lifespan was eighty years.
Question:
If this sutra clarifies permanence, what is the purpose of the *Nirvāṇa* [Sūtra]? Answer:
This has already been explained above.
Since the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* has already clarified the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), what further need is there for the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* to clarify it?
And since the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* clarifies the understanding of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), what further need is there for the various *Prajñāpāramitā* scriptures to clarify it?

Furthermore, if that were the case, then since the third period contains only the *Vimalakīrti* to clarify the principles of suppression and exaltation, would the *Sāgaranāgarājaparipṛcchā-sūtra* not be rendered useless?
Question:
What is the difference between these two sūtras regarding their clarification of the eternal?
Answer: This sutra directly clarifies two meanings: first, the provisional and the real of the teaching; second, the true and the responsive aspects of the body.
By briefly expounding these two, the assembly will readily understand.

The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* explains in detail the four virtues, the three dots, and the two causes—the conditioned and the direct; therefore, while its phrasing differs from this sūtra, its meaning is the same.
Question:
Although you have explained in various ways that the Buddha is eternal, this has merely clarified his eternity from the perspective of principle.
Furthermore, since the Buddha himself spoke of impermanence in this sūtra, one should not contradict the sūtra by asserting that it is permanent.
As the sūtra says, "Twice the number above," which implies there is ultimately a limit; therefore, it is ultimately impermanent.
Answer: This sutra clarifies that he has long since attained Buddhahood; this means he has long since realized the eternal.
At the time of realizing the eternal, it is still beyond the knowledge of those in the position of a successor (anujāta).
Regarding the statement that "now it is twice the aforementioned number," how could this be known after one has realized the eternal?
If even those who exhaustively study it do not know, then only a Buddha perceives it; for the Buddha’s lifespan is immeasurable, and therefore he is eternal.
Furthermore, the statement that the number is "twice as much as the former" is intended to explain the Buddha’s meaning of being without beginning or end.
Previously, it was clarified that he attained Buddhahood long ago, yet Maitreya did not perceive its beginning; this clarifies the meaning of being without beginning.
Now, by stating that the number is again twice as much, it is shown that Maitreya does not perceive its end; this clarifies the meaning of being without end.
Question: For what reason is it explained that there is no beginning or end? Answer:

The "Chapter on the Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa" also uses a specific event to secretly manifest that there is neither birth nor extinction; now, by means of the metaphor of subtle atoms, it clarifies that there is neither beginning nor end.

This is because his body, being without birth or extinction, differs from the bodies of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles, and his lifespan, being without beginning or end, differs from the lifespans of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles.

Because the bodies of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles are subject to the transformation of arising and ceasing, their lifespans have a beginning and an end, being destroyed within a single period; therefore, the Tathāgata’s body is neither born nor extinguished, and his lifespan has no beginning or end.

Furthermore, Dharma Master Zhao’s *Nirvāṇa-śāstra* precisely elucidates these two meanings: "The six realms of existence have no means to encompass its arising, and the power of karma has no means to transform its substance. This refers to the absence of arising and ceasing.
"Following it, one finds no trace; meeting it, one beholds no head"—this clarifies its lack of beginning or end.

Master Zhaol did not see the *Nirvāṇa* or *Avataṃsaka* sūtras, yet he drew from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Prajñāpāramitā* to compose this treatise; thus, it accords with the intent of those scriptures.
Question:
This scripture merely clarifies that his attainment of Buddhahood was long ago; how can it be said that he has neither beginning nor end? Answer:
Now, let us examine the intent of the sutra in detail.
If it were merely to clarify that [the Buddha] attained Buddhahood long ago, what benefit would this ultimately provide for sentient beings?
The reason for this is that both initial attainment and long-term attainment are impermanent; what advantage, then, is gained by now opening up the perspective of long-term attainment?

Now, to deeply grasp the Buddha’s intention: his manifestation began at Gayā and concluded beneath the twin trees; thus, this was a lifespan subject to impermanence. Those in the position of succession did not see its beginning, and those who have mastered all learning do not know its end; only a Buddha perceives a Buddha, for his lifespan is immeasurable.
Examining the intent of this text, how could it not be entirely true?
The three examinations become ever more manifest, and upon further reflection, the matter is already resolved.
Thus, the *Dharmapada-śāstra* states: "The phrase 'twice the aforementioned number' indicates the manifestation of the Tathāgata’s eternal life."
"It is because they employ skillful means to manifest a multitude that exceeds the aforementioned numbers, such that they cannot be known.
Upon seeing this passage, both sorrow and joy welled up within me.
I asked again:

If one were to take recent attainment as the skillful means (*upāya*) and long-standing attainment as the definitive teaching (*nītārtha*), then while the *Lotus Sūtra* clarifies that long-standing attainment is this definitive teaching, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*’s exposition of the initial realization of perfect enlightenment as the skillful means would be untenable. Thus, it cannot be so.
Furthermore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "Having heard half a verse, I shall transcend nine kalpas of Maitreya and attain Buddhahood first.
I now ask: is this statement of transcending nine kalpas a literal teaching or a provisional one?
If this were the definitive teaching, then the *Lotus Sūtra* would be a provisional teaching.

Furthermore, if the "leaping over nine kalpas" were the definitive teaching, since various Hīnayāna sūtras and śāstras also clarify the leaping over nine kalpas, it would follow that the Tripiṭaka constitutes the definitive teaching and the *Lotus Sūtra* is a provisional scripture.

If one were to say that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* clarifies that [the Buddha's] long duration is real while the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* clarifies that the transcendence of nine kalpas is provisional, then the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* would be the reality and the *Nirvāṇa* would be the provisional.
Furthermore, since the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* has already revealed the "near," how could the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* again conceal the "far"?
If the meanings of the "near" and "far" in these two sūtras were mutually interchangeable, then the same would have to apply to the doctrines of the "three" and the "one."
He asked again:

"If the *Lotus Sūtra* reveals the near to manifest the far, clarifying that [the Buddha] attained Buddhahood long ago as the fundamental reality (*mūla*) and his recent attainment as the manifested trace (*vyañjana*), why does the 'Chapter on Never-Disparaging' further conceal the far to clarify the near, and obscure the fundamental to distinguish the trace?"
Within a single sūtra, there should be no contradiction between what precedes and what follows.
If, within a single sūtra, the provisional (迹) and the fundamental (本) are sometimes concealed and sometimes revealed, then the three and the one may either coincide or not.

Furthermore, if this sutra were a literal teaching intended to clarify that [the Buddha] had already attained Buddhahood long ago, then the initial revelation of the Three Vehicles to manifest the One would be common to all Buddhas, whereas the revelation of the near to manifest the far would be unique to Śākyamuni alone.

If one were to take this meaning as an illustration, then in the following "Chapter on the Distinction of Merits," all the bodhisattvas make the vow: "May my exposition of the lifespan in the future also be like this."
"How can one say that only Śākyamuni reveals the near to manifest the distant, while other Buddhas do not?

Examining these various matters in detail, we know that this merely relies on the absence of beginning and end to manifest the meaning of the eternality of the Dharmakāya; all instances of having a beginning and an end are merely manifested traces (nirmāṇakāya)."
Applying this principle to all the aforementioned sutras, there is not the slightest obstruction.
This meaning is difficult to clarify; it shall be discussed more extensively in the sections on the "Original and Traced" (Honji-Suijaku) and the "Chapter on the Lifespan" (Juryōbon).

Furthermore, regarding the scriptural evidence for impermanence provided by the statement that [the lifespan] is "twice as much again" as the aforementioned number, there are two passages in the sutra: the first passage clarifies that the lifespan remains constant and does not perish for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, while the latter passage clarifies the phrase "twice as much again."
If you consider what was stated later to be impermanent, why do you not take what was proven earlier as permanent?
Question:
Why are the preceding and succeeding statements contradictory?
Answer:

The subsequent passage cites the cause to explain the effect, clarifying that even the lifespan attained while practicing the bodhisattva path has not yet come to an end; how much less could the lifespan of a Buddha ever be exhausted?
If even when one occupies the rank of a crown prince one's resources are not yet exhausted, how much more so when one ascends the throne of a Heavenly Son—how could one's emoluments ever be depleted?
Question:
Why is it that within the causal state, lifespan cannot be exhausted?
Answer:

From the stage of the ten faiths up to the ten bhūmis, as practice becomes profound, one's lifespan likewise becomes immeasurable; how much more so, then, could the age of the Dharmakāya ever be exhausted?

Furthermore, for one who asserts that what is necessarily impermanent is permanent, this person would, according to reason, obtain boundless merit; for the Buddha’s teachings are fundamentally intended to reveal the underlying principles.
If one asserts that what is eternally abiding is impermanent, one incurs immeasurable sin.
As the *Śāstra* says: "In reality, there are no Buddhas of the ten directions; yet by respectfully speaking of their existence, one obtains merit."
"Buddhas truly exist in the ten directions; to say they do not is to incur a great transgression.

Now it is clarified that this sutra represents the ultimate Dharmakāya, which is neither "not-not" nor "is-is"; it is no different from the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Since it cannot even be called "permanent," how could it be said to be "impermanent"?
Therefore, it is called "wondrous fruit.
Because both cause and fruit are wondrous, it is termed the "Wondrous Dharma" (Saddharma).
Next, the meaning of "lotus flower" (padma) is explained.
Some say: In foreign lands it is called *puṇḍarīka*, which here is translated as "lotus flower.
There are four colors of lotus flowers; setting aside three and taking one, the white lotus is called *puṇḍarīka*.
"White" is the fundamental among all colors; it is also a metaphor for the wisdom that is white, pure, and equal.
Question:
For what reason is the Buddha-eye compared to the blue lotus?
Answer: Blue represents the color of the Buddha-eye; it is taken as a metaphor because of its similarity.
White is the root of all colors, signifying that the One Vehicle is the root of the Three Vehicles; therefore, white is taken and not the three [colors].
The commentary states: Not so.
"Lotus" (padma) is a general name, whereas "Puṇḍarīka" is its specific designation.
How is this known? Master Yuì’s preface states:

"Among all flowers, the lotus is supreme. When the flower has not yet opened, it is called *kumuda*; when it has opened and is about to fall, it is called *kamala*; and when it is in its full bloom at the midpoint, it is called *puṇḍarīka*."
Master Yuan said: "Puṇḍarīka is the name for the lotus when it is in full bloom.
However, as the substance of this flower changes with the passage of time, its name shifts accordingly."

When it first emerges but has not yet opened, it is called *kuvalaya*; when it is fading and falling, it is called *mṛdita*; and when it is fully blossomed, possessing exquisite color and fragrance, it is called *puṇḍarīka*.

The sixteen-fascicle *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* explains the ten titles [of the Buddha], stating: "A *puṇḍarīka* lotus among men. Since both names appear together, there must be a distinction between the general and the specific.
Furthermore, four types of lotuses are enumerated, the last of which is called the *puṇḍarīka* flower; Daolang of Hexi described it as "a brilliant white.
Elsewhere, it is translated as "the red-colored, most fragrant lotus."
Now, it is explained that among all flowers, the lotus is supreme; and among lotuses, the *pundarīka* is the most beautiful. Therefore, it is called the *pundarīka* flower.
Furthermore, a verse in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* asks: "How can one dwell in a turbid world without being defiled, like a lotus?
The subsequent "Bodhisattva Chapter" answers this by citing four types of lotuses; thus we know that "lotus" (*padma*) is the general name, while "puṇḍarīka" is its specific designation.
Now, using the general term for translation, it is called "lotus flower.
If it has not yet opened, there is only the cause and no fruit;
if it has already fallen, there is only the fruit and no cause.

Now, taking the correct opening [of the sūtra], the cause and effect are clearly distinguished: the flower is a metaphor for the cause and the fruit is a metaphor for the effect; the flower is a metaphor for the teaching and the fruit is a metaphor for the principle.
Question:
For what reason does the Sanskrit original employ its specific designation, *puṇḍarīka*, while here in this land we retain its general name, "lotus flower" (*padma*)?
Answer: *Puṇḍarīka* must necessarily be a lotus flower; here we take the *puṇḍarīka* lotus, which is not distinct from other lotuses.

Furthermore, in foreign lands this flower has three different names according to the seasons, whereas here there is no corresponding threefold seasonal translation; therefore, its general name is retained, which thereby encompasses the specific meanings as well.
Question:
For what reason is the metaphor of the lotus used for this sutra? Answer:
Briefly explaining sixteen meanings:

first, it clarifies that this flower is the foremost among all flowers. The *Śāstra* states: "Among land-born flowers, the *sumanā* is the foremost; among water-born flowers, the blue lotus (*utpala*) is the foremost."
By this analogy, it is shown that among all sutras, this sutra is the most supreme.
Therefore, it is said below: "That which the Buddhas have taught, are teaching, and will teach—this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the most profound and subtle."

Question: It has already been stated that "what has been taught" refers to the period prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, namely the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other such scriptures; "what is to be taught" refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* itself; and "what follows" refers to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* and other such scriptures.
For what reason is it said that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is the most difficult to believe and understand? Answer:

Although all Mahāyāna sūtras reveal the Way as being ultimately without difference, prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the Great and Small Vehicles were divided into separate streams; following the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the convergence of the three vehicles was finally completed.
However, this sutra marks the beginning of the reversal of the three and the initial step toward returning to the one; therefore, it is the most difficult to understand and is called the foremost.
Second, it clarifies that these flowers grow from seeds, serving as a metaphor for how the One Vehicle arises from conditions.
Therefore, the following verse states: "The Buddha-seed arises from conditions; for this reason, the One Vehicle is taught.

This third point clarifies that these flowers have their time for opening and closing: when they open, it is day; when they close, it is night. This serves as a metaphor for the One Vehicle having its time of concealment and manifestation: it is concealed because the great conditions are not yet mature, and it is manifested because the conditions have matured.
Fourth, it clarifies that this flower can serve as an auspicious sign, illustrating that upon seeing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, one knows for certain that all sentient beings will attain Buddhahood.
